thesis: In Western Europe the dissolution of serfdom after the Black Death (c. 1348–1500) was driven primarily by the demographic collapse that raised the bargaining power of peasant labour; but because the identical demographic shock entrenched a second serfdom in Eastern Europe, the divergent outcomes show demography operated only through pre-existing balances of class and political power, not as an autonomous cause.

positions.name: Neo-Malthusian demographic / factor-price (Postan)
positions.gist: Population collapse after the plague altered the land-to-labour ratio, automatically raising real wages and dissolving serfdom as a factor-price response, with demography the prime mover of medieval economic trends.

positions.name: Class-power / Political Marxism (Brenner)
positions.gist: Divergent outcomes flowed from the balance of class power and social-property relations, not demography: the same shock cut both ways because the structure of class power determines how demographic and commercial changes take effect.

positions.name: Commercialization / Smithian (Pirenne)
positions.gist: The revival of long-distance trade, towns, the bourgeoisie and a money economy dissolved feudal bonds, letting serfs buy commutation or flee into urban freedom, so capitalism grew quantitatively out of commerce.

positions.name: Neoclassical property rights (North & Thomas)
positions.gist: The manor was an implicit labour-for-protection contract; when plague made labour scarce, changing factor prices and transaction costs led Western lords to compete for tenants and commute dues to wages, while Eastern lords colluded to re-enserf.

positions.name: Crisis of feudalism / falling feudal levy (Bois)
positions.gist: A structural contradiction between small-scale peasant production and large-scale seigneurial property produced a secular tendency to a falling rate of feudal levy, an internal law of motion that broke the system independently of Brenner's class-struggle voluntarism.

positions.name: East-Elbian second serfdom (Malowist, Kula, Blum)
positions.gist: East of the Elbe the same demographic shock intensified serfdom because the Baltic grain export trade, weak dependent towns, and a strong cohesive nobility let lords expand coerced demesne (Gutsherrschaft) labour rather than free it.

positions.name: State formation / market integration (S.R. Epstein)
positions.gist: The late-medieval crisis was an institutionally induced integration crisis of jurisdictional fragmentation and coordination failure, not a Malthusian ceiling; post-1350 state-building lowered transaction costs, integrated markets, and enabled Smithian growth.

benchmark_claims.claim: Share of Europe's population killed by the Black Death (c. 1347-1351)
benchmark_claims.value: about 45-50% over four years; overall estimates range 30-60%

benchmark_claims.claim: Statute of Labourers enacted to cap post-plague wages
English farm wages after the plague
benchmark_claims.value: farm wages in England roughly doubled between 1350 and 1450 despite wage-capping legislation

benchmark_claims.claim: Collapse of English seigneurial rent revenue after the plague
benchmark_claims.value: revenues from peasant lands fell by as much as 55% between the 1380s and the 1420s
